title: Ben Webster as a person and shared western tastes
summary: Leeman calls his time with Webster a musical romance despite Ben's heavy drinking, and says they bonded over western boots, a Mexican saddle and horseback riding.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong

blocks.x: I know you'd be interested to know, Milt,

that our bass player -- I forgot to mention him, was Billy Taylor, Jr., he was a young man then with a wonderful talent, and I'm sure you would agree with me. That's before he moved to Washington, D.C. -- and in the past year or so, he passed away.

My association with Ben Webster was a musical romance. I use that expression to show my admiration and love for many of the great instrumentalists I worked with. But this one was special, very special. And I had a great love for Ben Webster as a person. He was unbelievably heavy in his drinking towards the latter years, and it just utterly destroyed him. Many people talked of his mean disposition when drunk. Well, to me, he was beautiful, and as the saying implies, seeing and believing is in the eyes of the beholder.

You will appreciate knowing this information, and my final episode in his quartet. I was instrumental in Ben's seeing and joining a new set of values in recreation. Number one, we were heavy drinkers, or we had a drinking problem, as well as mutual admirers of musical taste. Second, he couldn't get over the fact that I had a beautiful pair of hand made western boots, cowboy heels, and a beautiful Stetson and rancher's twilled pants that I carried on the road with him, anyway, a huge Mexican goat skinned and hand-tooled show saddle. A bridle and breast plate, all with silver spangles. He was a farm boy, originally
and he said he used to ride as a kid. I told him I rode some and broke some ponies that my father had as a hobby for show purposes at county fairs, in Maine.
